scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The courante emerged in the late Renaissance as a couple dance among the social elite, initially danced with fast running and jumping steps as recorded by Thoinot Arbeau in 1589.

During the Baroque era, it evolved into an instrumental and theatrical staple of the suite, splitting into a solemn, complex French style and a faster Italian corrente before disappearing from active social use by the late 18th century.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed during opulent court balls and theatrical ballets as an aristocratic social exercise.
In the Baroque suite, it bridged the measured Germanic allemande and the meditative Spanish sarabande, embodying a psychological landscape of sweet expectation, longing, and serious reflection.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Danced by couples, the traditional Renaissance and early Baroque courante utilizes combinations of 'simples' and 'doubles' executed with a slight spring or jump (*pas sauté*).
The French Baroque style emphasizes a moderate, majestic tempo with hemiolas and crossed accents, while the Italian corrente favors a faster, more continuous flow.
Watch for Pas sauté, Hemiola cadence.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Couples traveling along the perimeter of the hall, turning, and executing advances and retreats.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Composed in triple meter with an upbeat (levée) and structured in binary form with repeats.

Instruments of the Baroque court and chamber—such as violins, harpsichords, lutes, and small ensembles—played the repertoire, which ranged from Bach's intricate keyboard partitas to Lullian orchestra pieces.
Listen for the violins, harpsichord, lute.
The pulse is Triple metre (typically 3/2 or 6/4 for French; 3/4 or 3/8 for Italian).
A triple-meter texture beginning on an upbeat, characterized by shifting metrical accents, graceful counterpoint, and an interplay between solemn dignity and buoyant forward momentum.

Listen later: Partita for Violin No. 2 (Corrente) — Johann Sebastian Bach; Partitas for Clavierübung — Johann Sebastian Bach

scenes.title: The people
narration: Thoinot Arbeau, Cesare Negri, Johann Mattheson, Johann Gottfried Walther, François Couperin, and Johann Sebastian Bach.
The two primary historical variants are the French courante (slower, 3/2 or 6/4 meter, complex hemiolas) and the Italian corrente (faster, 3/4 or 3/8 meter, more direct melodic flow).
Descended from Renaissance couple dances and branles; ancestral or peer movement to the allemande, sarabande, and minuet within the Baroque suite.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Courante is sibling of allemande: Typically precedes the courante as the first or second movement in a Baroque dance suite.
Courante is sibling of sarabande: Typically follows the courante in the standard sequence of a Baroque suite.
